results.title: Nebius Group: A layman's explanation
highlights:
How they charge for it

Nebius sells the same underlying product (GPU time) in three ways:

1. On-demand, pay-as-you-go. A customer swipes a card and rents GPUs by the hour with no commitment, at published list prices. As of mid-2026 those published rates run roughly $3.85/hour for an older-generation H100 chip, $4.50/hour for the newer H200, and $5.50–$7.15/hour for the latest B200. This is the smallest, most competitive, most price-sensitive slice of the business because dozens of competitors publish similar rate cards, and customers shop around.
2. Committed/reserved contracts. Here a customer commits to a volume or duration in exchange for a discount off the list price. Nebius advertises discounts of up to 35% for larger, longer commitments. This is the bulk of the mid-market and enterprise business (companies like Cursor, Shopify, Cloudflare).
3. Dedicated capacity contracts. The largest customers (e.g. Microsoft, Meta, etc.) usually don’t rent shared GPU-hours at all. They’ve signed multi-year contracts (Microsoft up to ~$19.4B, Meta up to ~$27B) that reserve entire blocks of Nebius’s future capacity for their own exclusive use, often prepaying a meaningful chunk upfront. This is less “renting a hotel room” and more “leasing an entire floor for five years.”

Across all three, the price is not set of off the costs, but to whatever the market for that chip generation will currently bear, which is why Nebius management keeps saying demand exceeds supply: as long as four or more customers are competing for every GPU that comes online, Nebius has pricing power and doesn’t need to discount.

...

Purpose-built for AI vs. retrofitted hyperscaler infrastructure

There is another important difference to grasp. Nebius is what is known as a “neocloud” which means that they are specialized for AI, whereas the big dogs, Azure, AWS, etc. are known as “Hyperscalers”. For AI, being a neocloud is a real and meaningful advantage, not just marketing.

...

From the broader market

- Spot GPU rental rates (H100/H200) for the older chips — fastest-moving real-time signal, on-demand market is around $3 - $3.6 and is flat for about a year which is a strong indication that older chip prices are holding because demand is still high
- Hyperscalers’ capex guidance (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta) — broad deceleration would matter more than any one company

results.title: GPU Cloud vs Hyperscaler: The 2026 AI Infrastructure Cost Comparison
highlights:
Neocloud pricing for H100 GPUs ranges from $1.80/hr (marketplace) to $3.50/hr (on-demand), while hyperscalers charge $6.88–$12.29/hr for equivalent silicon. A 40–85% gap. But egress fees, idle time, and architectural lock-in can erase those savings entirely for workloads that don't match the pricing model. The provider that minimizes total cost depends on whether you train, serve inference, or both, and whether your workload tolerates interruption.

...

The gap isn't an edge case. Saturn Cloud's June 2026 report on 17 GPU cloud providers found that self-service H100 pricing spans roughly $1.80–6.16/hr depending on provider and commitment level, compared to $6.88/hr, $10.98/hr on GCP, and $12.29/hr on Azure. That is a three-to-six times difference for the identical NVIDIA GPU hardware. CoreWeave charges no egress for any data transfer. Crusoe charges none either. The hyperscalers charge $0.08–0.12/GB for data leaving their network, a cost that can add 20–40% to a monthly bill for data-heavy pipelines.

But the neocloud story is not uniformly cheap. Several raised published on-demand H100 rates in early 2026: Lambda went from $2.99 to $3.99–4.29/hr; Verda (formerly DataCrunch) moved from $2.29 to $3.25/hr. Nebius held steady at $2.95/hr. The blanket assumption that neoclouds undercut hyperscalers is now provider-specific. Check before committing, and verify that the published rate reflects actual availability rather than a theoretical list price with no real inventory behind it.

| Provider | H100 On-Demand | H100 Spot | Egress | Billing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CoreWeave | ~$3.50/hr | N/A | Free | Per-hour |
| Lambda Labs | $3.99–4.29/hr | N/A | Included | Per-hour |
| Nebius | $2.95/hr | N/A | Free | Per-minute |
| Spheron | $2.50/hr | $1.03/hr | Included | Per-minute |
| AWS (p5) | $6.88/hr | ~$3.83/hr | $0.09/GB | Per-second |
| GCP | $10.98/hr | N/A | $0.12/GB | Per-second |
| Azure | $12.29/hr | N/A | $0.087/GB | Per-hour |

As of June 2026. Spot pricing available where providers publish it. Sources: Saturn Cloud GPU Cloud Comparison Report, Spheron pricing data, provider published rates.

...

CoreWeave, the largest pure-play neocloud, went public in early 2026 with a $99.4 billion revenue backlog. Its strategy is hyperscaler-grade infrastructure without the hyperscaler margin structure. It offers InfiniBand clusters, VAST storage integration, and NVIDIA's full GPU stack from H100 to B200. It charges roughly $3.50/hr for H100 on-demand, with no egress fees. The trade-off: its pricing model rewards reserved commitments, and on-demand availability can be tight during peak demand.

Lambda Labs built its reputation serving academic and research teams. Its on-demand H100 PCIe runs $3.99–4.29/hr, up from $2.99/hr in late 2025, a 33–43% increase that reflects tightening supply. Lambda operates its own fleet, which means when inventory fills up, customers wait. The company's 3-year reserved contracts bring H100 cost to $2.43/hr, but locking in for three GPU generations in a market where NVIDIA refreshes architecture annually carries depreciation risk.

Nebius, the European neocloud, holds at $2.95/hr for H100 on-demand with per-minute billing, the most aggressive pricing among the three. Its $17.4 billion Microsoft contract, signed in late 2025, signals that even hyperscalers are outsourcing GPU capacity to neoclouds. Nebius bills per minute rather than per hour, which for short-duration workloads (preprocessing, hyperparameter sweeps) can cut costs by 30–50% vs per-hour billing.

results.title: GPU Price Data: Free Daily Snapshot, API & Licensed History
highlights:
Prices checked 13 November 2026

# GPU rental price data: downloads, API and citation

Every price on this site, free to download and reuse with credit: 594 offers from 37 providers across 53 GPU models, and a daily, append-only record kept since 5 July 2026 (132 days). No account and no key.

...

| What | Format | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Today's prices | CSV | One row per offer, the eight fields below. |
| Like-for-like price change | CSV | Every on-demand configuration behind the like-for-like change on the statistics page, with its price on both days. |
| The index by month | CSV | The GPU Rental Price Index and the typical on-demand rate of every GPU, month by month since 5 July 2026: monthly average, change on the month before, like-for-like change, daily range, providers and whether the month is final. Each row links its sentence on the month's page. |
| Daily price history | CSV | The cheapest price of every GPU on every day since 5 July 2026, with its provider and billing type, and whether that day's price was carried forward from a failed check. The series the history page and the GPU pages chart. |
| Today's snapshot | JSON | Every offer with all published configuration fields (node size, region, stock, CPU, RAM, commitment), plus each provider's check status. |
| Price changes feed | Atom | The biggest price drops and rises of the latest seven days (one entry that always covers the latest week; earlier weeks are not kept) and each monthly market report, for a feed reader. No sign-up. |
| Collection health | JSON | Snapshot date, offer and provider counts, and which providers' checks failed. |
| Corrections | JSON | Every correction to the daily record: provider, GPUs, dates, what was done, why and the day it was recorded; the file's `updated` field is the day of the newest. |
| Archived first weeks (5 to 18 July 2026) | Zenodo | A fixed copy of the daily files from 5 July 2026 to 18 July 2026, with a permanent identifier, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21435394. It is not updated: for later days use the downloads above, and cite them with the text under "Licence and citation". |

...

## What each field means

`date`
: The day of the price check (UTC) the row belongs to.
`provider`
: The provider's identifier, as in the provider page address (runpod, lambda, voltagepark…).
`gpu`
: The exact GPU variant, from our registry (h100-sxm, a100-pcie-80, rtx-4090…).
`vram_gb`
: Memory per GPU in GB, as the provider lists it.
`usd_per_hr`
: The price per GPU per hour in US dollars, before storage, data transfer and tax.
`kind`
: Billing type: on-demand, secure (a provider's datacenter tier), community, spot, marketplace, reserved or serverless.
`source_url`
: The provider's own page the price was read from.
`fetched_at`
: When we read it (ISO 8601, UTC). A provider whose check failed keeps its last date; it is never shown as today's.

A price is per GPU. Where a provider sells only whole nodes, the snapshot's `min_gpus` gives the smallest node and the node price is the per-GPU rate times that count; where a provider publishes no node size, the field is absent rather than assumed to be one. Stock is recorded only where a provider reports it and is never inferred from a price. How we collect, check and rank is set out in the methodology.

...

## Badges

Each GPU with a current on-demand price has a live price badge (36 today) for a README or a dashboard, for example `https://gpurentalprices.com/badge/h100.svg`, which shows the cheapest on-demand H100 rate and links back to its page when you wrap it in a link. A GPU without a current on-demand price (listed only as spot, community or serverless capacity, or not listed today) has no badge.

results.title: Together AI and the margin test inside the GPU-hour
highlights:
On the other side, raw GPU markets keep setting a floor. Together's pricing page listed on-demand GPU cluster rates at $3.99 per GPU-hour for HGX H100, $5.99 for HGX H200 and $8.19 for HGX B200, with lower H100 rates for longer reservations in the visible table: https://www.together.ai/pricing. Its dedicated endpoint docs listed single-GPU H100 at $6.49 per hour, H200 at $7.89 and B200 at $11.95, billed per minute while the endpoint is running, regardless of request volume: https://docs.together.ai/docs/dedicated-endpoints/overview. Those figures show why utilisation matters. A dedicated endpoint is attractive when a customer values isolation, latency and control; it is wasteful when demand is spiky and idle minutes dominate.

Competitors create price pressure from several directions. Lambda's public pricing page listed H100 cluster plans at $6.16 per GPU-hour for a 16-GPU two-week-to-one-year plan, falling to $5.54 at 256 GPUs, plus applicable sales tax: https://lambda.ai/pricing. CoreWeave's public pricing showed NVIDIA HGX H100 systems at $49.24 per eight-GPU hour, or roughly $6.16 per GPU-hour before other service differences, with spot at $19.71 per system hour: https://www.coreweave.com/pricing. Nebius docs listed NVIDIA H100 NVLink from June 1, 2026 at $3.85 per GPU-hour and preemptible H100 at $2.15 in the region where it is available: https://docs.nebius.com/compute/resources/pricing. Runpod's pricing page showed a live GPU marketplace with B200 at $8.64 per hour and H200 at $5.93 per hour on the visible serverless pricing block: https://www.runpod.io/pricing. AWS Capacity Blocks listed single-H100 p5.4xlarge examples at $4.326 per hour in several US regions and $3.933 in several non-US regions, while the AWS P5 page frames H100 and H200 EC2 instances for deep learning and high-performance computing: https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/capacityblocks/pricing/ and https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/p5/.

The comparison is not apples to apples. Some offers include managed orchestration, some require whole nodes, some are interruptible, some are tied to specific regions, and some bundle support or software differently. But the implication is clear: Together cannot rely on GPU scarcity alone. It has to earn a spread through performance, developer experience, model availability, data controls, reliability, support and workflow integration. If a customer can achieve the same throughput and latency with a cheaper raw GPU rental plus an open-source serving stack, Together's margin compresses.

results.title: Cloud’s Hidden Memory Bill - ONE2CRYPTO
highlights:
On January 4, 2026, AWS announced a roughly 15% increase in GPU instance prices, with specific instances like the eight-H200 jumping from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour. This marks AWS’s first price hike since the cloud service’s inception.

The price increases are driven by a 60–70% rise in DRAM prices at the manufacturing level, affecting server costs across the industry. OEMs such as Dell, Lenovo, and HP have responded by raising server prices by 15–25%, which in turn raises the cost for cloud providers.

The ripple effect has led to a 5–10% increase in cloud instance prices for consumers, particularly impacting memory-optimized instances and in-memory services like Redis and ElastiCache. These are most sensitive to DRAM cost hikes due to their high memory usage.

...

AWS raised prices for the first time in its history — ~15% on GPU capacity; its 8×H200 instance went $34.61 → $39.80/hr. OVH forecasts +5–10% by Sept; the others stay silent but buy from the same OEMs. The precedent is the story: once the door opens, it doesn’t close.
